Another issue concerns the consumer of the research. I've seen others in the situation where their results did not conform to the client's (or management's) beliefs. I don't agree that all research is suspect. But all research has weaknesses, and it's best to be aware of that and look out for them.

The freehold mineral titles are not as attractive as Crown leases at the moment.  The Crown leases, I understand, delay the royalty payment until drilling costs are recovered.  Royalty on a freehold lease starts with the first dollar of production.  
There is a freehold mineral tax (FMT) on productive wells which works out to about 5% of net royalty.  (Basic exemption for marginal wells so the resource is extracted rather than abandoned).   If the oil and gas company defaults on the payment of the surface lease for the well site, the farmer can apply to the Alberta government to receive payment in lieu.  The FMT is assessed on the owner, not on the well operator.  If a company chooses not to pay the tax, the freeholder pays or forfeits title. 
This FMT does not apply to Crown leases.  Freehold mineral owners may watch their resource drained away from wells on crown leases without any compensation as the Crown royalty rate is usually lower than freehold royalty plus FMT.

Two years ago, I took the MOOC “Technology Entrepreneurship” put on by the Stanford engineering school. The course leader (a Stanford prof) brought out many good points. I consider that the most important were the business model (how do you make money), the size of the market and its potential to go viral. 

I chose a case close to my experience, an electronic market for truckers of shipping containers to and from ports. Business model: booking service fee, which may meet resistance. Market size: about 700 million containers transit ports, but each market is local and much smaller. Viral: only within local markets. So not worth pursuing.

Compare with Uber in its better days: simple fee for service, all people in the world who need transit, every private vehicle in the world and high potential to go viral, in part because an app that works in LA can work in London.

Note in both cases: no R&D required at the outset, just a good idea. R&D can come later for apps and algorithms.

It ensures that the elected chamber has the final say as it should.

There is a difference between pain and suffering, and this is part of the confusion over pain control. Pain is the actual physical sensation, and certainly can be excruciating, which is what narcotics are for. Suffering includes pain, but also includes all the emotional turmoil that surrounds it. So someone who has fibromyalgia, for example, may also experience depression because of loss of independence or inability to work, anxiety related to inability to accept the diagnosis, thinking perhaps that the pain is due to undiagnosed cancer, or frustration at friends or family who may not seem to appreciate the sufferer's distress. None of the latter can be helped by narcotics, but if the only question the health practitioner asks is "do you have pain?" the answer will always be "yes", and the danger is that the dose of pain medication will continue to be increased even although that will only add to the individual's problems rather than relieving them.

Once you understand how the Canadian stumpage system works, it's hard not to see it as a government subsidy to the industry and workers.  Rather than auction off timber rights, under stumpage the BC government collects fees based on the lumber companies' difference between production cost and selling price.
Under an auction-based system (used in the USA), the lumber companies bear the risk of price fluctuations.  If prices drop due to excess supply, they are incented to reduce production.  However under stumpage, the Canadian producers have no incentive to reduce production, and their profit levels are assured, because if the lumber prices drop, the stumpage cost drops so they remain whole.  It is an insurance scheme for industry profits - they have transferred the risk to tax payers. I completely agree. The Jones Act is the sole reason for the very high cost of living here.

For those not familiar, the Jones Act is a protectionist law that says any ship traveling from a U.S. port to a U.S. port must be an American-made ship with a majority American crew. So, a ship bringing goods to the U.S. from China is not allowed to stop in Hawaii, drop off part of its load, then continue on to another U.S. port. Since Hawaii's demand for goods is small (relatively speaking) what this does is forces ships to go past Hawaii to drop their goods on the Mainland. And goods that need to then go to Hawaii are offloaded from that foreign-flagged ship, loaded onto another U.S. flagged ship and then sent to Hawaii. Since over 80% of U.S. goods carried over water are on foreign-flagged vessels, and U.S. ships are generally much more expensive to operate, this more than doubles shipping costs to the islands.
